forestry-002: The Nan'ao Historic Trail lies in Jinyang Village, Nan'ao Township. It is one of the paths to old Atayal settlements, part of the former Wuta Historic Trail and a traditional Atayal hunting ground. From the ruins of the Xuantan police post it follows the Nan'ao South River upstream to the end of the trail, where the Heliu River joins the Nan'ao South River — 1.5 km in all. The route is gentle and easy, rich in wildlife and plants, with relics along the way such as the ruins of a suspension bridge and the roadbed of an old guard road.
forestry-004: The Jinguāliao Fish Fern Trail is in Pinglin District, New Taipei, with entrances at both its north and south ends. It has an arched bridge, a viewing deck and quite a few steps; continuing south past the south exit links up with the Fish-and-Fern Trail managed by the Pinglin District Office. The whole route winds along the babbling Jinguāliao Creek, where you can spot Taiwan shovel-jaw carp and Taiwan stream carp, along with many kinds of ferns — a good outing for families.
forestry-005:
Quantoumu Mountain, a little over 300 m high, stands in the Tiansongpi area of Sanxing Township, Yilan. The trailhead is at km 9.5 of Provincial Highway 7C. The gentle trail runs through a plantation of Michelia (wuxin) trees, rich in ferns and varied plants that change with the seasons and give birds and small creatures a good home. From the summit you look down on the Lanyang River and Lanyang Plain, with the Central and Xueshan ranges in the distance.

The trail was once an overgrown forestry road. The Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency restored it with nature-friendly methods and added a viewing deck, turning it into an eco-trail through the Michelia and incense-cedar plantations of compartment 47, Luodong working circle. Named after its fist-shaped summit, it opened in mid-September 2007.
forestry-006:
The Songluo Trail was rebuilt from an old Atayal hunting path. It follows Songluo Creek under deep shade, with the sound of running water and lush epiphytes — its signature feature. The low altitude and humid conditions create a primeval, rainforest-like landscape. Songluo Creek keeps you company the whole way, and you can clearly see the results of recent conservation: Taiwan's native fish swimming freely. Most striking are the moisture-loving plants and animals found nowhere else on this scale — dense tunnels of bird's-nest ferns, wide carpets of ferns and dragonflies everywhere — it feels like the Amazon.
To protect the original ecology, the trail was built from local materials and avoids artificial ones as much as possible, so it is especially comfortable to walk and blends into the beautiful natural setting.
forestry-007:
The Paoma (Horse-running) Historic Trail was once used by early settlers to carry goods and by Japanese troops for patrols and supply runs. It has since been renovated and widened, but some of the old log sleepers and wooden sledges used for hauling remain, so even at today's leisurely pace you can sense the hurried, tireless steps of those who came before and appreciate how hard early pioneering in Taiwan was.

As soon as you enter the trail you feel a cool breeze and the fresh scent of the forest. The path is wide and gently sloped, mostly gravel, with stretches overlooking the Lanyang Plain and Guishan Island, abandoned mine entrances, citrus orchards and streams — great for the whole family.
forestry-008:
The Linmei Shipan Trail shows off a low-altitude subtropical valley. Built along an old irrigation channel, it is now wide, gentle and easy while keeping its old-world charm. Shady woods, running water and fresh forest air make it a refreshing family walk.

The name combines Linmei Village in Jiaoxi Township and Shipan Falls. Along the way you'll see streams, waterfalls, pools of all sizes and gorge scenery — it's nicknamed "Yilan's little Taroko". When sunlight filters through the leaves the light is enchanting, and tree frogs and insects often rest on the foliage — a trail full of the lively breath of nature.
forestry-009: The Holy Mother Mountain Trail climbs above the Wufengqi Waterfall scenic area in Jiaoxi Township, Yilan. It is a Catholic pilgrimage route and a waypoint toward Sanjiaolun Mountain, one of Yilan's five great peaks. The viewing deck at the end sits on the Yilan–Taipei boundary, with the Lanyang Plain to the east and the layered ridges of the Xueshan Range to the west; on the windward ridge a green sea of arrow bamboo sways and rustles in the wind — so beautiful you won't want to leave.
forestry-011: The Xinliao Waterfall Trail starts from Zhongshan Village in Dongshan, Yilan, and follows the Xinliao Creek valley upstream for 1.2 km. Faults in the area have created several waterfalls. The forest is varied and full of life, with running water, frog calls and birdsong — ideal for families. The first 0.9 km is fairly flat; after that, stone steps get steeper but reward you with more rapids and slanting falls.
forestry-012: The trail follows the creek and stays warm and humid all year. Jiuliao Creek gathers wild streams from below Quantoumu Mountain in the Xueshan Range; its water is plentiful, clear and almost as cold as a spring, and it forms grand waterfalls where it crosses faults. The trailhead is in the Jiuliao Creek Ecological Park run by the Datong Township Office. The whole route is a flat dirt-and-gravel path that leads easily to the falls, under dense shade thick with epiphytes and ferns.
forestry-013: The Taiwan Beech Trail is one of the longer trails in Taipingshan National Forest Recreation Area. The first section is fairly flat but muddy after rain; after 2.5 km the gradient varies more — mostly downhill on the way out and uphill on the way back. Along the way are forestry relics such as old cables, railway roadbed and track switches, as well as slate cliffs, green moss, red cypress, Japanese cedar and mountain cherry. The rest deck at the end looks across to Taiwan's largest primeval beech forest on Tongshan; in autumn the leaves turn gold and draw many visitors.
forestry-014: The Cuifeng Lake Loop Trail circles Taiwan's largest alpine lake and was built along an old logging railway, offering fresh greenery in spring, misty rain in summer, red leaves in autumn and snow in winter. The lake sits at 1,840 m and spreads to 25 hectares in the rainy season; it changes from dawn to dusk and has a different charm every season.
forestry-016: The Maoxing Nostalgia Trail begins at Maoxing station of the Taipingshan Bong-Bong train and follows the old train track. It is gentle, with good rest facilities and interpretive signs throughout, and you can combine the main line with upper or lower loops. This logging railway, built in the Japanese era, winds through red cypress, Taiwan cypress and Japanese cedar, lined with shade-loving shrubs, ferns and ground cover. It passes through forest, around cliffs and over streams, and the old rails and workers' huts bear witness to Taipingshan's logging heyday.
forestry-018: The Hemlock Forest Nature Trail lies in the transition zone between mid-altitude conifer and broadleaf forest. Its height and exposure to ocean currents make moisture condense, so it is wrapped in mist all year like a fairyland; it is also the water source for Taipingshan Villa. Ancient trees tower overhead and the air is soft and damp. The entrance is behind the Cypress Primeval Forest Trail above the villa, so you first climb the villa's 400 central steps, lined with red-leaved maples — a stunning red tunnel. Along the way are dense stands of primeval red cypress and Taiwan cypress; leaning and fallen giants form remarkable hollows and tangled roots.
forestry-019: This 0.9 km trail is gentle, with wooden benches for resting — suitable for all ages. As you enter the Jianqing Historic Trail you'll see the old forest railway that once carried Taipingshan's timber, surrounded by ferns and moss-covered trees and cool, damp air. There are occasional viewpoints from the start; on clear days you can see the Lanyang Plain and the Holy Ridge, and sea-of-clouds views often appear in the afternoon. In the later section an elevated stretch of railway shows fine craftsmanship weathered by time, stirring a sense of nostalgia.
forestry-020: The trail is in the Jiuzhize area of Taipingshan National Forest Recreation Area, across the Duowang River from the Jiuzhize hot springs and linked by the Duowang suspension bridge. A mild climate, plentiful rain and valley terrain nurture rich and varied life, and there are good rest facilities along the way. Surrounded by mountains and crossed by the river, the area forms a wetland full of birds whose calls never stop — hence its name, "Turtledove Marsh".
forestry-021: Wangyang Mountain rises to 2,050 m. A viewing deck at the end of the trail has a fine outlook over the valley carved by the Nan'ao North River, and it's a great spot for sunrise and seas of clouds; before full daylight you can even see the night lights of the Lanyang Plain. Looking out to the Pacific from the trail, Guishan Island is clearly visible on fine days.
forestry-022:
The Chaoyang Trail is on Guishan hill in Nan'ao, Yilan. Guishan is a lone hill south of the Chaoyang community, with the Hualien–Taitung coast to the east and rolling farming and fishing villages to the west; from afar it looks like a sea turtle resting between the mountains and the sea, hence its name.

The trail was once the main path early settlers used to farm the hills. Four viewing decks, each higher than the last, look down on Nan'ao fishing harbor and out over the Suhua coast, Wushibi Cape, Dingqing Lake, Yuanyang Mountain and a hidden beach, with waves and sea breeze all the way.

You can also see a rare 7-hectare pure stand of Gordonia trees and century-old plum trees. Climbing Guishan for the sunrise and the sound of the waves is the most delightful part of the walk.
forestry-023: A hiking route between Dongyanshan and Manyueyuan national forest recreation areas. It starts at the end of the Dongyanshan forest road (870 m), crosses the 1,130 m saddle between North Chatianshan and Dongyanshan, then drops to the Manyueyuan waterfall area at about 500 m. The main path uses old handcart and timber-sledge roads joined to the trail from Manyueyuan to North Chatianshan. It lies in the low-to-mid-altitude evergreen broadleaf belt of laurel and oak; mixed conifer and broadleaf forest forms a closed canopy rich in birds and insects, with cloud falls, streams and waterfalls — a pleasant hike in northern Taiwan in any season.
forestry-024: The Fuba National Trail runs from Fushan in Wulai to Lalashan in Baling, passing through the Lalashan giant-tree area and the Chatianshan Nature Reserve. Many giant red cypresses line the route, and it is an important habitat for wildlife with rich biodiversity. The trail was once an Atayal path for hunting, marriage and visiting relatives; in the Japanese era a guard line and police road were built here, and ruins of police posts remain.
forestry-025:
North Chatianshan, also called Takai Mountain, is a well-known mid-level peak in the northern Xueshan Range and the source of the Yunei River, a tributary of the Dahan River, in Yisheng Village, Fuxing District, Taoyuan.

Its steep, upright shape sits in the cloud belt; when mist rises it looks like a peak thrust upside down into the sky, hence the name "Sky-piercing Mountain". Its temperate forest holds countless breathtaking giant trees and large pure stands of beech. In spring and summer the green forest is full of birdsong; in late autumn the beech leaves turn gold and drift down; in deep winter the silver rime in the forest and the white Holy Ridge in the distance are spectacular.
forestry-026:
Syakaro is the Atayal word for the Michelia (wuxin) tree, which grows abundantly here. The trail crosses Wufeng and Jianshi townships in Hsinchu and was the main route linking local communities with the outside world. The Syakaro National Trail is a dreamlike historic trail of history and scenery: along it are ruins the Japanese built to subdue the communities of Jianshi and Wufeng — police posts, utility poles, bunkers, monuments, earth walls and gun emplacements. Interpretive signs tell the many moving stories behind this trail.

The scenery is beautiful — suspension bridges, mountain streams and forest — and the bamboo groves of Liyuan and sweetgum forest of Ma'an are especially charming. There are many excellent maple-viewing spots; in autumn the hills blaze red, making it a well-known place to see autumn colors.
forestry-027:
Dabajian Mountain (3,492 m) in the Xueshan Range is one end of the Holy Ridge. Its grand, unusual shape has earned it the name "Peak of the Century", and it has long been sacred to the Atayal and Saisiyat peoples. With sheer cliffs on all sides it looks like a giant wine barrel, so it is also called "Wine Barrel Mountain"; together with Zhongyangjian and Dafenjian it is one of Taiwan's "Three Spires".

The trail reaches four of Taiwan's Top 100 peaks: Jiali, Yize, Dabajian and Xiaobajian. Jiujiu Cabin, at about 2,700 m, is the key base camp on the route, a comfortable place to stay and a fine spot to enjoy the Guanwu area, sunsets and starry skies.
forestry-028:
The Tonghou Crossing Trail crosses the Xueshan Range straight from Greater Taipei into Yilan. It isn't difficult and can be done in half a day. The Tonghou River's varied terrain shows completely different scenery in different stretches — as the saying goes, "if you haven't been to Tonghou, you don't know how beautiful Taipei's rivers are."

One of the three great historic trails of the Wulai mountains, it was the route the Atayal took north from the Xueshan Range to hunt and migrate; today it is a popular hiking route.
forestry-030: The Red River Valley Crossing Trail was once the route between Jiajiuliao in Wulai and Xiongkong in Sanxia. It follows the Xiongkong and Jiajiuliao creeks.
forestry-031: The Hapen Crossing Trail links New Taipei and Yilan, following the Nanshi River upstream toward the Lumen and Hapen creeks. The rebuilt trail ends where it meets Lumen Creek and returns the same way — about 14 km round trip, taking 6–7 hours. Below the trail runs the Nanshi River; the broadleaf forest, draped with bird's-nest ferns and ribbon ferns, forms a subtropical landscape. Ruins of an old guard road remain at the end.
forestry-034: Taman Mountain is New Taipei's highest peak at 2,130 m. The route is lush and dense, with oddly shaped trees, towering giants and many fallen logs that show the forest's cycle of life and decay. The path is mostly tangled roots and dirt; the small summit has no view.
forestry-035: Bei Delaman is a traditional hunting ground the local Atayal regard as sacred, and one of Taiwan's rare red cypress forests below 1,000 m. The forest changes with altitude — from plantations to natural broadleaf forest and the cypress belt — and its varied plants support abundant animals. You'll find fruit dropped by animals on the trail; flying squirrels are most common in the broadleaf forest and are a highlight of the community's eco-tourism. Along the way are an echo valley and a small waterfall. At 1.6 km a loop drops to the giant trees, where you can see four huge red cypresses known as the "Four Heavenly Kings".
forestry-036: The Maliguang Waterfall Trail is short, gentle and charming, with rich vegetation and views of the valley winding through green hills. After about 10 minutes you hear the roar of water: a white ribbon about 80 m high and 30 m wide plunges into a deep emerald pool. Benches on the viewing deck let you sit and enjoy the mighty falls, the misty air and the sound of running water.
forestry-038:
The Atayal call the Cinsbu (Zhenxibao) community a place where "the sun is already shining while you sleep, the sunlight lasts until dusk, days are warm and nights cold, free of pests, where crops grow well." It holds Taiwan's largest primeval cypress forest, facing the Smangus giant trees across the Takejin River and joining the Qilan cypress forest toward Yuanyang Lake in Yilan.

The best-known giants are the "Adam" and "Eve" trees, whose forms vividly resemble male and female anatomy. The massive "King" tree ranks 17th among Taiwan's giant trees.
forestry-042: On the south bank of the Wenshui River, this mountain looks like a giant eagle, its flanks like wings and its pointed summit like a beak — hence "Bird's Beak Mountain". With nearby Henglong and Huzi mountains it forms a phoenix, dragon and tiger trio known as the "Three Stars of Shuiyun". Also called Shangdao Mountain, its geology means the 3.3 km one-way trail climbs 837 m, so it is steep and demanding. The route passes cedar plantations and broadleaf forest; the summit has a fine view of Jiali, Hakanni, Henglong and Huzi mountains.
forestry-043:
The Jiali Mountain Trail links Penglai, Fengmei and Luchang in Nanzhuang, through Japanese cedar plantations and broadleaf forest with ferns and shade-loving plants beneath; Fengmei Creek runs through it, rich in wildlife.

Old logging handcart rails along the way recall the forestry boom. Jiali Mountain is a well-known peak of north-central Taiwan with a first-class triangulation point; the broad summit view takes in the majestic Holy Ridge of Xueshan and nearby Luchang Mountain.
forestry-044: Wuzhi (Five Finger) Mountain is named for its five peaks lined up like fingers. Famous since the Qing dynasty, it was described in the Tamsui Gazetteer as "fingers piercing the clouds" and listed among the region's eight sights; in the Japanese era it was voted one of Taiwan's twelve scenic wonders. The trail is lined with Japanese cedar, green and serene. Its striking peaks drew many temples, including Yunguang Temple, Yuhuang Palace and Guanyin Chan Temple. The summit view takes in Emei, Beipu, Hsinchu and Zhubei.
forestry-046:
The Dongguashan Trail is on Xishui Mountain, commonly called Winter Melon Mountain. The trail doesn't reach the summit; it ends at a thousand-year-old zelkova.

The area is mostly Japanese cedar plantation — tall, straight trees in a dark, closed forest. New leaves in spring turn yellow and red in autumn, and after they fall in winter the trees look like giant brooms. Hakka farms at the foot of the mountain grow peaches and plums; in blossom season the green mountain stands out against a sea of red and white flowers. Through the trees you glimpse Hushan, Shangdao and Jiali mountains, and now and then a towering crape myrtle or zelkova.

A nearly vertical rock wall is a highlight; beyond it are a few small landslides and gravel slopes that are safe with care. At the end the thousand-year zelkova suddenly appears — not as big as Alishan's sacred tree, but the largest known zelkova in Taiwan; even a big person looks small beside it.
forestry-047:
The Malabang Historic Trail was used by the Atayal Beishi group for travel and hunting, and in the Japanese era became a guard road. An Atayal uprising against Japanese rule took place here, marked by a memorial. The trail passes cedar plantations and zelkova groves, with peach blossoms in spring, green bamboo in summer, red maples in autumn and plum blossoms in winter. From the summit you can see the winding Da'an River, Dabajian Mountain and the Holy Ridge to Xueshan.

Malabang is rainy in summer and autumn and dry in winter. The traditional route starts at the Shanghu trailhead and climbs to the battlefield memorial at about 1,250 m; maple and sweetgum forests stretch to the spot hikers call "Qingrong Pass", red with autumn leaves in late autumn.

At 0.7 km from the Natural Lake trailhead is a Taiwan zelkova mother-tree forest planted in 1944. Its leaves change through the year — red buds in spring, green in summer, brown-gold in autumn, bare in winter — one of the region's signature species for autumn colors.
forestry-048:
The Henglingshan Nature Trail was a timber-sledge road used by Daxueshan residents in the Japanese era to haul logs, one of the old sledge routes of the Daxueshan forest farm, so it is also called the Henglingshan Timber Sledge Trail. Abandoned sledges and ruined charcoal kilns remain along the way, and only the stone foundation is left of a workers' hut at km 2.3 — witnesses to the logging era.

The trail is 6.6 km long, rich in wildlife and beautiful forest, running from the Henglingshan tunnel at km 26.5 of the Daxueshan forest road to the Daxueshan eco-classroom. The first 3.5 km is gentle under towering trees, soft underfoot with pine needles. After 3.5 km it gets steep, dropping more than 2,000 eco-steps built of sleepers and sandbags. Near km 4 is a forest of Taiwan's endemic rhododendrons. Returning the same way means climbing those 2,000-plus steps, so arranging a shuttle between both ends is easier.
forestry-049: Daxueshan National Forest Recreation Area was an important logging farm in central Taiwan during the Japanese era; its grasslands reportedly reminded the Japanese of Daisetsuzan in Hokkaido, hence the name "Daxueshan". Climbing the Daxueshan forest road from Dongshi, the forest changes with altitude from broadleaf to mixed and then natural conifer forest. Being in the cloud belt, the weather changes constantly. The area has many trails, each with its own charm through the seasons — alpine flowers in spring and summer, changing leaves in autumn and winter — and it is one of the best places to stargaze.
forestry-050: Baxianshan National Forest Recreation Area sits on an alluvial terrace where the Shiwen and Jiabao rivers meet among layered mountains — the former Jiabaotai branch of the Baxianshan forest farm. Its broad river terrace, green forest and cool climate made it a well-known resort in central Taiwan. The mixed conifer and broadleaf forest supports rich birdlife and insects, with something special each season: mountain cherry blossoms in January–February, tung blossoms in April, fireflies in March–April and butterflies from June to September. Many logging relics remain along the trails, including reservoirs, dormitory foundations and a torii site.
forestry-051: The Defulan Trail is behind the Songhe Defulan community in Bo'ai Village, about a three-hour walk. Most of it follows a Taipower maintenance road along the foot of the great southeastern landslide face of Dongmao Mountain, with the Dajia River to the east. You pass steep rock walls and scattered boulders, sometimes scrambling over stacked rocks using hands and feet; stone steps made from local rock have an old-world charm. Giant Machilus, zelkova and bishop-wood trees and thick climbing vines are the trail's main features.
forestry-052: Baxian Mountain, about 8,000 Japanese feet high, was first to be named "Baqian (8,000) Mountain" before the more elegant "Baxian (Eight Immortals)" was chosen. Leader of the Seven Heroes of Guguan, it takes about 8 hours round trip at hiking pace. The first half is steep; once on the ridge it eases off. The whole route is shaded, passing from evergreen broadleaf forest into mixed forest with clear seasonal change and colorful scenery year-round.
forestry-053: Dongmao Mountain (1,692 m), fifth of the Seven Heroes of Guguan, was originally a Taipower maintenance road. The scenery is lovely and the ecology rich and varied. The trail climbs in gentle, wide switchbacks — an easy mountain to get to know. The broad summit has a large microwave reflector and a superb 360-degree view; on clear days you can see the Songhe community and the ranges of Yuanzui, Shaolai, Malun, the Baxian ridges and Tangmadan.
forestry-054: The Tangmadan Mountain Trail is on the south bank of the Dajia River. It is last and lowest of the Seven Heroes of Guguan, but the climb from trailhead to summit is over 650 m, so it is still quite challenging. The trailhead is in the Lileng community. The summit has the best view of the seven: Baxian and Malun to the east, Baimao and Aleng to the west, and Dongmao and Wuwowei to the north. A side trail leads to Butterfly Valley Falls if you have the time and energy — it is the only one of the seven with a waterfall.
forestry-055: The Bojinjia Trail is on the north bank of the Dajia River, fourth of the Seven Heroes of Guguan. It was once a Taipower maintenance road, and old fallen wooden poles and anchor cables can still be seen beside the path. The name is said to come from hikers describing it as "so steep!" (a pun in Taiwanese). With about 1,000 m of elevation change, nearly the whole route climbs; allow 7–8 hours round trip.
forestry-056: Wuwowei Mountain, on the north bank of the Dajia River, is third of the Seven Heroes of Guguan. The trail passes varied habitats — rhododendron woods, low wind-swept forest on the ridge, cedar plantations, mixed forest and laurel-oak forest; clusters of mushrooms grow on damp fallen branches and leaf litter. On clear days, gaps in the trees reveal the surrounding mountains.
forestry-057:
Malun Mountain extends west from Baigu Mountain in the Xueshan Range and is second of the Seven Heroes of Guguan, a well-known mid-level peak in central Taiwan. The first 1.8 km and the branch to the Eight Warriors giant tree were once called the Sikeba Trail — an Atayal hunting ground and an old timber-sledge road of the Xinshan forest farm; the path to Malun was built by Xinshan workers to carry supplies.
President Chiang Kai-shek once inspected the area and ordered the trail renovated and widened, keeping logging relics and adding pavilions and viewing decks.
The trail is lined with Taiwan red pines and carpeted with pine needles and maple leaves, soft and springy underfoot; in autumn the red leaves make it look like a red carpet. Passing the century-old "Mother" five-needle pine, you can hear the pines roar like waves and smell their resin in the air. A viewing platform beside the trail overlooks Guguan and the graceful mountain skyline — arguably the most beautiful trail in the Guguan area.
forestry-059: Baimao Mountain, on the south bank of the Dajia River, is sixth of the Seven Heroes of Guguan, with a triangulation point at about 1,522 m and one of the rarer views among the seven. Secondary broadleaf forest and large Japanese cedar plantations draw many large mammals and birds to feed. Parts of the trail are steep; a landslide area before the summit marker overlooks the Dajia River and Guguan's Dadao Temple, with views of Dongmao and Tangmadan mountains. A wooden pavilion on top offers a place to rest.
forestry-060: The Yuanzui–Shaolai National Trail is a popular mid-altitude route in central Taiwan. Yuanzui and Shaolai can be hiked separately: Yuanzui is known for its sheer cliffs, Shaolai for the Taiwan red maples that cover it in autumn; walked together, the route offers continuous cliffs and beautiful scenery. Chuanxing and Anma mountains lie in Daxueshan Forest Recreation Area on the final ridge of the Xueshan Range, linked by the Shaolai–Xiaoxueshan National Trail — about 10 km from the trailhead near the km 35.2 ticket booth to the Xiaoxueshan visitor center parking lot at km 49.
forestry-061: Hehuan Jianshan (3,217 m) is one of the Hehuan peaks but not on the Top 100 list. Its pyramid shape, like a math-class model, is unforgettable — a horn peak carved during the Ice Age by glaciers scouring in different directions. The trail is short but rises abruptly and steeply: the north side has new wooden boardwalk steps, the south side is rock and dirt among jagged stones and arrow bamboo, with no tall trees for shade; some stretches need ropes and hands. The small summit has a great view of the Hehuan peaks and distant Central Range mountains such as Qilai Main and North peaks.
forestry-062: Hehuan East Peak (3,421 m) is No. 35 of Taiwan's Top 100 peaks; the trailhead is behind Songxue Lodge. Each season looks different — wildflowers in spring, lush green in summer, bleak in autumn and snow in winter. The trail passes the densest stands of Yushan rhododendron; in May and June the slopes are dotted with pink blossoms. A ski training ground once operated on the gentler east side of the peak, and an abandoned lift station can still be seen.
forestry-063:
Taoshan Falls is one of Taiwan's six great waterfalls; Taoshan (Peach Mountain) is named for its peach-like shape when seen from afar.

The trail is fragrant with pine and shaded all the way, like a forest from a fairy tale. It climbs gently past the Wuling suspension bridge, which turns fiery red in autumn, while the Formosan landlocked salmon — a national treasure — swims below. Viewpoints along the way look out to Taoshan and the Xueshan Range and down over all of Wuling. The falls at the end, once called Yansheng Falls, are at 2,500 m and about 80 m high, spectacular after the rainy season. At the base, look for its old name carved in the rock, now fading.
forestry-064:
The Nenggao Crossing Trail crosses the Nenggao mountains to link both sides of the Central Range. The west section is in Ren'ai Township, Nantou, the east section in Xiulin Township, Hualien. It was originally a Seediq migration and trade route.

In the Japanese era, to exploit Taiwan's forests and control the mountains, the Japanese built the Nenggao Crossing Police Road. It first ran from Wushe over the Liandai saddle to Chuyin, and was later rerouted over the saddle between Nenggao and Nanhua (Nenggao North Peak), the route known today.

After 1945 Taipower widened it into a maintenance road for carrying electricity from east to west and laying phone lines — a major contribution to western Taiwan's industry and daily life. To commemorate this, Taipower erected the "Guangbei Babiao" monument at the Nenggao saddle, inscribed by President Chiang Kai-shek. Since 2002 the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency has protected the route as a national trail, and it has become a popular hike.
forestry-066: The Nenggao Crossing Trail is 26.5 km long, measured from the Tunyuan trailhead in Nantou (km 0) to the east trailhead (km 26.5). The Guangbei Babiao monument at km 15.5 is where the trail crosses the Central Range and divides the west and east sections. The east section therefore runs 11 km from the east trailhead at 1,582 m up to the monument at 2,787 m, climbing 1,205 m past Wujiabeng Mountain, the Huilin maintenance station and the Upper Huilin suspension bridge.
forestry-067:
The Taoyuanli Forest Trail lies on the southern slope of the Bagua Mountain Great Buddha scenic area, near Sanqing Temple, Bagua Chan Temple, Cihui Hall and Dongshan Chan Temple. Made up of the forest, Longfeng Valley, Youlan Valley and fitness trails, it is the local residents' backyard for walks and exercise.

There are cable bridges, fitness areas and viewing decks along the way. The plants are varied: white tung blossoms in spring followed by golden acacia flowers, fragrant star fruit, longan and lychee orchards in summer, and an eco-garden that draws birds, insects and butterflies. Around Qingming, flocks of grey-faced buzzards pass over the Bagua range on their way north, making this a prime spot for bird and raptor watching.
forestry-069: The Qingshuiyan trail network beside Qingshuiyan Temple in Shetou Township, Changhua, has three trails — the Eighteen-Bend Salt Carriers' Trail, the Central Ridge Plantation Trail and a connecting trail. With beautiful forest and moderate difficulty, they form a complete network with varied scenery.
forestry-070:
The Qilinshan Forest Trail is behind Zantian Temple and Puxing Temple in Tianzhong Township, Changhua. The Nantou branch rebuilt it with nature-friendly methods, deliberately keeping the large trees and routing the boardwalk around them — a clever, playful design.

There are viewing decks, pavilions and outdoor fitness equipment along the shady, scenic route. The boardwalk runs between a deep ravine and a valley; from the ridge you see the vast acacia forest to the south and the cliffs and gullies of badland terrain, and to the west, downtown Tianzhong and the Changhua Plain. With little elevation change, it's an easy loop back to the start — good for families of all ages.
forestry-072: The Kengneikeng Forest Trail was an old pilgrimage path residents used to reach Shoutian Temple on Songbo Ridge, linking Changhua and Nantou counties. Along it are an eco-engineering display area, an ecological observation area and a viewing deck. Every March the golden trumpet trees bloom, forming a golden tunnel hundreds of meters long — its signature sight.
forestry-075:
The Seshui Forest Trail is in the Seshui community beside the Dayan Tunnel, southwest of the Zhongtan Highway in Yuchi Township, Nantou. It starts beside Jintian Temple and passes the community's main crop — tea — along with lush forest, natural wetlands, waterfalls and streams.
With the upper Taomikeng Creek and Seshui Creek flowing through, it is rich in frogs, birds, mammals and insects.
forestry-078:
The Longguomai (Dragon Crossing) Forest Trail links Linzhong, Linnan and Pingding villages in Linnei Township. Linnei's hills join Caoling and the layered peaks of Zhushan in Nantou, connecting with Chukou and Dongjia mountains. Legend says that looking down from the Caoling–Zhushan border, the ridge looks like a dragon's back, and where the Zhuoshui and Qingshui rivers meet it looks like the dragon drinking — hence the name.

The trail is rich in natural and cultural sights. From the Tieguankeng entrance you first pass Linnei Park, once a Shinto shrine, where a torii still stands quietly. On the dragon's back the ridge has fine views over Yunlin and the Bagua range. Dropping into the shade, the natural low-altitude secondary forest is full of life — you may meet crested serpent eagles, Formosan macaques or the rare fairy pitta, and in spring beautiful swarms of purple crow butterflies. An approachable dragon with both history and scenery, great for families.
forestry-079:
The Erlun Nature Trail lies in a 27-hectare protection forest west of Provincial Highway 19, known as Lot No. 4 in the Japanese era. Sand from the riverbed built up into dunes over the years; today it is a green eco-trail park.

The trail rises and falls with the dunes — walking on soft golden sand is a special experience. Along the way are an asparagus-fern boardwalk, a suspension bridge, a lake-view deck, an outdoor insect classroom, a "breathing" pavilion and rest areas. The boardwalk is lined with asparagus fern, known as bride's grass, for a romantic feel, and plant signs make it educational. At the end the lake-view deck looks out over the water; return by another path to complete a relaxed loop suitable for all ages.
forestry-080: Big Tashan, together with Little Tashan to the west and several other peaks, forms the Tashan range, sacred to the Tsou people. The trail starts beside the younger of the Sister Ponds and at first runs alongside the Alishan Forest Railway. The first 2 km is an easy sleeper boardwalk through towering cypress forest — a refreshing forest bath — and the last 1.5 km climbs steeply. The viewing deck at the summit has a 360-degree view over the whole Alishan Forest Recreation Area and the magnificent Yushan peaks.
forestry-081:
The Tefuye Historic Trail in Alishan Township, Chiayi, was originally a Tsou hunting path. In the Japanese era its later section became the Shuishan logging railway, and many railway relics remain.
The first section along the railway is gentle and lined with beautiful Japanese cedar; the later section drops steeply down sleeper steps through primeval broadleaf forest that changes through the seasons, rich in wildlife — an excellent birding trail.
forestry-082: Named for where Chiayi, Nantou and Yunlin counties meet. Lush moso bamboo forest makes it lovely and shaded almost the whole way. Shibi Mountain and Cape of Good Hope offer superb views of layered mountains and the winding Qingshui River.
forestry-083:
The Ruitai Historic Trail, once called the Youha forest road, links Ruili and Taihe and is more than a century old.

Under the Qing emperor Guangxu, Han settlers traded hunting rifles, sickles and daily goods with local Indigenous people for land. As settlers increased, the trail was opened to link the villages, becoming the main route for migration and carrying farm produce. In 1931, under Japanese rule, it was improved so residents of Ruili and Taihe could carry produce and walk to school. The section via Moyoukeng, Hero Slope and the Demon Cave to Huitou Ridge dates from the 1870s; the section via Moyoukeng and Wangtian Cliff to Huitou Ridge was rebuilt in 1931. The whole trail runs through moso bamboo — peaceful when sunbeams slip through the gaps, with the bamboo rustling all the way.
forestry-084:
The Four Heavenly Kings is the collective name for Sitianhuang, Qingyuan, Dubi and Zhiniao mountains, said to guard the hills around Shuisheliao and Jiaoliping like four mountain kings; they are also called the "Peace in Four Seasons" mountains.

From the trailhead at Shuisheliao station, a little stream keeps you company between dense, green moso bamboo — quiet and secluded, sometimes dappled with light, sometimes misty, like a hidden paradise. The trail circles Sitianhuang Mountain, its high point at 1,458 m (no triangulation marker), with a rest deck in the bamboo. Along the way you can see the Alishan Forest Railway, the rustic Shuisheliao station, tea gardens, layered mountains and rolling seas of clouds.
forestry-085:
Among Chiayi's continuous mountains, Duli (Solitary) Mountain stands alone, hence its name. The trail began as an old path settlers used to carry daily necessities into the hills. In the Japanese era the Alishan Railway was built to carry timber, circling Duli Mountain three times to reach the top.
The old trail is now the Dulishan National Trail — easy and good for families, with streams, railway, tunnels and suspension bridges along the way. The railway spiraling up three times is a unique sight.
forestry-086: The Dulishan–Dalongding trail, also called the Hongnankeng Forest Historic Trail, runs from Fengtian Rock (874 m) in Hongnankeng to near the Dalongding guesthouse on the summit of Dalongding. About 1,550 m long, it passes betel nut groves and moso bamboo and takes about an hour one way. It's the longest section of the Dulishan historic trails, but from the plateau on top you look out over tea gardens in every direction, with wide-open views.
forestry-090:
The Shimenggu (Stone Dream Valley) trail is in Fengshan Village, Alishan Township, on the upper Shigupan Creek, a tributary of the Qingshui River. Water has scoured potholes into the sandstone riverbed, and the trail ends at a broad, flat slab of rock — a truly unique landscape.

The first part is flat and easy; at Lovers' Valley you can see a waterfall. With frequent rain and fog, the trees are draped in lichen and old man's beard, giving the deep, dense forest a primeval feel.
forestry-092:
The Tea Trail is part of the Dingshizhuo trail network, where tea gardens, Japanese cedar, and sedan-pole and moso bamboo forests meet in an unusual landscape. The first section is mostly bamboo — walk the bamboo paths and listen to the leaves sway in the wind with the insects singing along; it's so relaxing you won't want to leave.

The middle section is known for its tea gardens, among lofty, green mountains. Tall, straight Japanese cedars are the stars of the forest bath. Native to Japan, they grow fast and are valuable timber, and were an important plantation species in the Japanese era. Walking among them in the breeze with birds and insects singing, you soak up the phytoncides and the sounds of the forest and feel refreshed. Past the bamboo and tea gardens, the trail reaches its high point, Leye Mountain (Jiucenglongping, about 1,696 m) — an uplifting spot and the best place in Shizhuo to watch the sunrise.
forestry-093: The Duigaoyue trail starts where the Zhushan forest road (km 3.95) meets the Zhushan railway line and passes Duigaoyue station. Along the way are beautiful stands of red cypress, Taiwan cypress and fir. As you climb, a cliff in front of the Duigaoyue pavilion looks out to Shenmu Village in Xinyi Township and the Heshe valley. About 1.7 km of steep climbing or descending — a real fitness challenge!
forestry-094: After the Alishan Sacred Tree fell, the park's giant trees were gradually cared for to keep visitors from trampling the soil and to protect the giant red cypresses and their roots. The Giant Tree Trail was built in two sections winding among 36 giant red cypresses, letting visitors see the oldest and most vigorous cypresses in Alishan. Highlights include the Guangwu Cypress (Xianglin Sacred Tree), the Thousand-Year Cypress, the Tree Spirit Pagoda and Shenmu station.
forestry-095: The Erwanping trail, also called the Black Forest Trail, runs through towering, beautiful Japanese cedars and passes two memorials, to Shindo Kumanosuke and Ninomiya Hideo. The cedars were planted after Alishan's logging era ended. The forest is so dense that even at noon only half the sunlight gets through, and it's dim earlier and later in the day — hence the name Black Forest.
forestry-096:
The Shizilu–Laiji historic trail starts beside Shizilu station at about 1,500 m. Originally 5.4 km long, it was the Laiji residents' link to the outside world and has important historical value.
The Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency restored 0.7 km of nature trail near Shizilu, mostly dirt path and stone steps; the remaining 4.6 km is farm road descending to Laiji at 800 m. Along the way are Japanese cedar, makino bamboo, little bridges and streams, with rich wildlife.
forestry-098:
The Lijia–Shanmei trail, also called the Limei or Guishan historic trail, is in Alishan Township, Chiayi, linking the Tsou villages of Lijia and Shanmei. As early as the Qing dynasty, Han interpreters used it as a major route for trade with Indigenous people, and before roads it was the only route between Lijia, Shanmei and Xinmei.

It originally passed Lijia Gorge, Lijia Falls, Longfeng Valley, Xiangshan, the Zengwen River and Danayigu, about 5.6 km in all, but typhoons and earthquakes have destroyed several sections. Today you can only walk from Lijia to the Lijia Falls viewing pavilion at km 1.2.

Lijia Falls is 100 m high; from the pavilion you watch a white ribbon of water hanging on the cliff and plunging into the valley. Along the way you can see Xiangshan. Scenic, cool and easy — great for the whole family. You can also visit Lijia village while you're there.
forestry-099: The Fenrui historic trail links Fenqihu and Ruili, two famous scenic areas. In the Qing dynasty settlers carried goods along it to trade, and the remains of charcoal kilns, the Yin-Yang Temple and a Shinto shrine survive. From the red-brick steps in front of the train station, it links the village eco-loop and the giant-tree path, then the Fentai and Ruitai historic trails, winding through dense primeval forest and moso bamboo, with towering giant oaks of every shape along the way.
forestry-100: The summit of Dadong Mountain above Fenqihu has a viewing pavilion at nearly 2,000 m. On clear days the view is vast, reaching Alishan, Yushan, Zengwen Reservoir, Caoling and other sights around Chiayi; it's also a spot for sunrise, seas of clouds and sunset glow.
forestry-103: Tufei (Bandit) Mountain, also called Fanlu Mountain, is 794 m high. The trail is in the Gongxing community of Fanlu Township, Chiayi, about 0.85 km long. The trailhead is in Gongxing (Wainaoliao), and the high point is about 700 m.
forestry-105: Dadong Mountain (also written Dadong with a different character), on the border of Baihe District, Tainan, and Dapu Township, Chiayi, is 1,241 m high — a grand, broad mountain with a magnificent western cliff face. It's the highest peak in old Tainan County and one of Taiwan's Little 100 Peaks. Along the way you can see Baihe, Luliao Reservoir, and Chiayi's Renyi and Lantan reservoirs. A fire lookout tower built long ago to guard against forest fires stands on top, with wide views over the layered, deep-green Guanziling hills, the Guanziling hot springs and the Chianan Plain. The trail runs through low-altitude broadleaf forest, tall and lush in the warm, humid climate and rich in wildlife. In winter, come to see the plum blossoms, white petals drifting against the sunset — truly beautiful.
forestry-106: The Guanziling Biyun Temple–Water and Fire Cave trail starts at Biyun Temple's Hall of the Three Jewels and leads to the Water and Fire Cave, with green mountain views along the way. The Water and Fire Cave, where flames burn above a spring, is one of Baihe District's best-known sights.
forestry-107: The Kanding trail is only about 500 m long and takes about half an hour round trip. It's in the botanical garden behind Kanding Fu'an Temple, a lovely spot full of trees and birds.
forestry-108: Jilong (Chicken Coop) Mountain is one of the Guanling peaks, named because its summit looks like a chicken coop. It's about 2 km from the trailhead, with many spots along the way overlooking the Chianan Plain. A wooden pavilion stands on top. The last stretch before the summit is planted with plum trees; in early spring you walk beneath snow-white, fragrant blossoms.
forestry-109: Kantou Mountain (844 m) is among the hills around the Zengwen Reservoir catchment. The trail runs through dense, shady low-altitude broadleaf forest with rich vegetation, including more than four hectares of camphor trees. From the trail and summit you can see the villages of Dongshan and the Chianan Plain, and on clear days even the coast. After rain there are often seas of clouds and cloud waterfalls — beautiful.
forestry-114:
The Yuding trail is in Beiliao, Nanhua District, Tainan. It is 1.6 km long with about 1,470 steps, climbing from 170 m to 430 m, almost entirely on stone steps and log boardwalk.
Starting at Tianyan Temple, it runs through quiet, lovely forest that keeps its natural primeval ecology. Most precious are the native orange jasmine trees, including many thick, century-old ones — the trail's signature sight. A walk through the forest calms body and mind; it's a newly popular, relaxed health trail.
forestry-119: North Dawu Mountain is the last peak over 3,000 m at the southern end of the Central Range and one of Taiwan's Five Great Mountains. The local Paiwan people consider it sacred and call it Kavulungan. It holds Taiwan's largest area of primeval forest and rich biodiversity. From the old trailhead past Kuaigu Lodge and the Dawu Shrine to the summit is about 9 km with about 1,549 m of elevation change, all within the Twin Ghost Lakes Important Wildlife Habitat — the finest of southern Taiwan's natural scenery. Most stunning of all are the autumn and winter seas of clouds. In recent years typhoons and heavy rain have collapsed the trail bed in several places, with detours climbing around them; please take care of your safety.
forestry-120: The Liugui Guard Line was the first guard line built in southern Taiwan during the Japanese era. To stop Indigenous raids from hindering the Japanese camphor industry, a guard line and electrified fence were set up to protect camphor workers and Japanese, with a dense military presence — 53 police posts and 4 supervisory posts along the line, many of whose remains survive. It lies within Tengzhi National Forest Recreation Area and overlaps part of the park's Xishi Flower trail.
forestry-122: The entrance is at about km 23.6 of the Dahanlin forest road; the 2.7 km from there to the prefecture boundary is the Jinshuiying trail (west section). In 2015 Pingtung County designated it a cultural landscape under the Cultural Heritage Preservation Act.
forestry-125:
Shuangxi Arboretum is in Guanglin, in the northeast corner of Meinong District, near the famous Yellow Butterfly Valley at the head of the Meinong River. It's named for the two streams that meet around it. It began in 1935 as the Japanese-built Zhutoujiao Tropical Arboretum, 7.56 hectares where precious or valuable tropical tree species were introduced, collected and raised. After 1945 little replanting was done and human disturbance stayed low, so besides the original tropical species regenerating on their own, some Taiwanese secondary-forest species have moved in.

The trail is well equipped and signposted, ending at a viewing deck at the high point. Walking under the tall, cool, dense canopy at a slow pace and in good spirits makes for a wonderful forest trip.
forestry-127: Lingshan belongs to the Yueguang range at the tail of the Yushan Range, shaped like a crested serpent eagle, on the border of Qishan and Meinong districts in Kaohsiung. The village at its foot is where Meinong was first settled 300 years ago. The Lingshan trail is popular in Meinong and a favorite exercise spot for locals. The entrance is beside Leiyin Temple; the trail is densely shaded with beautiful forest, and a small earth god shrine on top looks out over downtown Qishan and the Meinong Plain — an uplifting view! Behind the shrine you can continue to the Rendou Mountain triangulation point among bamboo and trees — a very pleasant walk.
forestry-130: Liuyi Mountain, about 784 m high, belongs to the Wushan range of the Alishan Range and marks the border of Jiaxian in Kaohsiung and Nanhua in Tainan; it was already a popular hike in the Japanese era. The trail follows the ridge, modeled on the Japanese-era path and built with eco-friendly faux-wood posts. It has four entrances — from north to south Side, Gongguan, Baiye and Zixia — and the full traverse takes about three hours one way. The trail is surrounded by leased plantation land, densely shaded with many tree species and a different look each season — especially in winter, when the plum trees bloom, fragrant and dreamlike. To the west, east and south you can see Nanhua Reservoir, the Central Range and the Alishan Wushan range — wide views, great for sunsets.
forestry-131:
Weiliao Mountain is on the border of Sandimen Township, Pingtung, and Maolin District, Kaohsiung. The first half of the trail is farm road zigzagging up gentle slopes. In April and May, white tung blossoms fall like snow on the path, making a romantic white carpet; in June the acacias cover the hills in bright yellow puffball flowers.
After that the trail becomes a rougher mountain path through low-altitude broadleaf forest, with a few tall Trema trees among clumps of thorny and giant bamboo — you may even meet local Indigenous people out gathering bamboo shoots. The later section is long and steep, sometimes needing ropes — a challenge-level route among the Little 100 Peaks. The summit, with a second-class triangulation point, has no view, but there are many good viewpoints along the way over the peaceful farmland of Maolin, Liugui and Gaoshu.
forestry-132: The Fawan–Taiwu trail, once called the Pinghe historic trail, turns left at a fork near the old North Dawu trailhead and ends at a four-way junction: right leads to old Pinghe, straight on to old Fawan. The stretch from old Fawan to Lot 32 of the Pingtung working circle is private land. The forest is closed-canopy and rich in epiphytes, with views of the grand North Dawu Mountain along the way.
forestry-133: Lilong Mountain (about 1,062 m), one of Taiwan's Little 100 Peaks, is an extension of the southern Central Range and the only mid-altitude mountain over 1,000 m on the Hengchun Peninsula. Its geology is mostly thick sandstone, with towering sheer cliffs and fields of giant boulders. The summit has good views, making this a route of great variety. The first 1.5 km or so is private land. Currently you can only go as far as the steel trestle bridge at about km 2.2: Typhoon Krathon scoured its foundations, leaving it tilted and shifted and at risk of collapse, so it has been closed. Please do not risk crossing it or passing beneath it.
forestry-136:
Shimen Mountain (also called Shimu Mountain), 384 m high, was once a military base. The first half of the trail is now Indigenous reserve land; the second half is forest land managed by the Pingtung branch of the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency. To prevent landslides and manage the Sichong River, it was designated a soil-erosion protection forest in 1929 and replanted to keep its natural forest.
The trail is shaded throughout. In White Banyan Valley, the prop roots of white banyans create the spectacular sight of "one tree making a forest." It takes about half an hour from the trailhead to the viewing deck and about an hour to the summit triangulation point; the last 200 m are very steep, almost a scramble. Along the way you see Shimen village and the Sichong River. From April to July the Melastoma blooms, covering the hills in lively purple.
forestry-137:
Gaoshifo Mountain in Mudan Township, Pingtung, is 514 m high. Since it and Laofo Mountain are both on the Hengchun Peninsula and both have "fo" (Buddha) in their names, hikers call them the "Two Buddhas of Hengchun."

The trail is about 2.5 km long, gentle throughout with no dangerous terrain. The first 500 m is steeper and takes more effort; after that it eases off so you can enjoy the rich plants and animals. The forest is primeval, with many plants unique to the Hengchun Peninsula, and it's a hidden spot for butterfly watching — good for families. The flat summit has a triangulation point, but a pure stand of Gordonia partly blocks the view. Nearby you can visit Mudan Reservoir, the Shimen Battlefield trail and the Pingtung Shimen Mountain trail.
forestry-139:
The Jiaming Lake National Trail is part of the South Section 2 of the Central Range. The path is clear all the way, with rich and varied alpine scenery: Taiwan hemlock and fir forest, high peaks and deep valleys, cliffs and landslides, arrow bamboo grassland and summit ridges. Deer calling in empty valleys, linked peaks, winter snow, bright moonlight and starry skies have long drawn hikers.

The trail passes two of Taiwan's Top 100 peaks, each with its own character: Xiangyang Mountain marks the southern limit of the Central Range's alpine tundra, while Sancha Mountain is famous for its broad, magnificent alpine grassland and, not far off, sapphire-like Jiaming Lake.
forestry-140: Dulan Mountain, Taitung County's mountain, is the highest peak of the southern Coastal Range and one of Taiwan's Little 100 Peaks, rising grandly above the Beinan Plain. Moisture from the Pacific keeps it wrapped in cloud year-round, nurturing dense forest and very diverse plant life — ferns especially flourish. Its mysterious, ethereal atmosphere earned it the name "Beauty Mountain." Dulan Mountain is sacred to the local Puyuma and Amis peoples; along the way you'll see the "Puyuma" stone marker and many Indigenous sites. The ridge has wide views: on one side the towering Coastal Range, on the other the boundless Pacific. With luck on a clear day you can see Orchid Island and Green Island.
forestry-141:
The Malaolou trail is the water-intake route for Chenggong Township's catchment, so it was built with eco-friendly methods that don't pollute the water and are easy for people to walk.

The first third is flat and easy; after that it gets more challenging, with steep climbs, ducking through boulders and caves, and five or six stream and pool crossings. With its rich plant and animal life, take it slow and enjoy it. At the end, Rainbow Falls — one of Taiwan's ten famous waterfalls — throws a rainbow in the sunlight on its falling water, utterly beautiful.
forestry-147: Liyu (Carp) Mountain is named for its carp-like shape; also called Beinan Mountain and originally Aoyu Mountain, it's a park behind Taitung's old train station. Its trail has viewing decks laid out along the terrain — the carp's head, eye, back and tail — with excellent views over downtown Taitung and the Pacific. To the north you can see Dulan Mountain (sacred to the Puyuma), Monkey, Stone and Tiger Head mountains, the Liji badlands and the Beinan Mountain fault scarp (known as Little Huangshan); on clear days even Green Island and Orchid Island. Mountains and sea — a feast for the eyes. The trail is shady, with old trees, birdsong and flowers — the green lung of Taitung City — and historic sites including monuments, air-raid shelters, a martyrs' shrine, bunkers and gun emplacements. An excellent hiking trail in Taitung City.
forestry-150: The Dawu Sea-View trail is gentle and takes only about 30 minutes to walk. Known as "Dawu's back garden," it's close to the sea with the sound of waves all the way. With the mountains behind and the sea in front, the pavilion looks out over the Pacific and the mouth of the Dawu River. The forest is mainly low-altitude broadleaf; plant signs and nest boxes along the way help visitors get close to nature and learn more about its ecology.
forestry-152: Yuemei Mountain has the northernmost first-class triangulation point of the Coastal Range and is one of the Little 100 Peaks. Both ends of the trail connect to farm roads used by local residents. The south end is gentle and easy; the north end is primeval forest rich in wildlife — developed later, it still shows low-altitude broadleaf forest as it once was. Openings along the way look down on the East Rift Valley and the long Coastal Range.
forestry-153: The Antong Crossing Trail crosses the Coastal Range and was an important route for migration, trade and marriage between people on the east coast and in the East Rift Valley. It fell into disuse after highways opened in the 1970s. Because of its rich natural resources and historical meaning, the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency had experts survey and rebuild it, so people can again follow in their ancestors' footsteps on this trail linking mountains and sea.
forestry-154: The east section of the Batongguan Crossing Road runs from Pushige (today's Yuli) west to Dashuiku Mountain on the Central Range. The Japanese government built it from 1919 as a major mountain road to subdue the Bunun people of the Lakulaku River basin. Luming Suspension Bridge was first built in 1920; about 180 m long, it spans the Lakulaku River. In 2006 the Hualien branch rebuilt the farm road from the bridge to behind Zhuole Elementary School as a nature trail about 2.7 km long — a hiking route combining history and nature.
forestry-155:
The Zuocang trail on the western edge of Hualien City was originally a Taiwan Cement mining road, rebuilt by the Hualien branch as an eco-trail for walking and relaxing. Easy to reach and gentle to walk, it is richly planted with lush green lawns, and as it winds uphill you gradually look out over the whole Qilai Plain and the vast Pacific.
Beside the parking lot is the Sakul trail, a loop of about 1–1.5 hours — combine the two if you have time.
forestry-156: Liyu (Carp) Mountain is named for its shape, like a carp curled up, and is an approachable Little 100 Peak. Its trail system has six trails — fitness, birding, wild fun, climbing, distant view and picnic view — so visitors can plan by fitness and time. The trails run through low-altitude broadleaf forest and plantations; cherry blossoms in spring and Taiwan golden-rain trees in autumn color the mountain. Beside the trails, Liyu Lake with its mountain reflections and blue waters is counted among Hualien's eight great sights.
forestry-159: The Hutou (Tiger Head) Mountain trail is in the Ruisui hot spring area of Ruisui Township, Hualien, at the foot of Jiangbunan Mountain within the village. Except for a short steep start, it's gentle and easy throughout. In low-altitude hills, it has broadleaf forest, bamboo and sweetgum, rich wildlife and good views over the East Rift Valley — great for family hikes and nature watching.
forestry-164:
Jiujiu Feng (Ninety-Nine Peaks), made up of many sharp, separate peaks, is also called Jiujiu Jianshan or Huoyan (Flame) Mountain, because from afar it looks like leaping flames. Its unusual geology makes it one of Taiwan's three great "flame mountain" landforms, along with Huoyan Mountain in Sanyi, Miaoli, and the Eighteen Arhats Mountain in Liugui, Kaohsiung, and it's the top sight in Caotun, Nantou.

The trail has north and south entrances — boardwalk at the south, concrete farm road at the north — and can be walked as a loop. It winds up the ridge between tall trees; open spots look out over Wufeng in Taichung, Pinglin and Shuangdong in Caotun, the Wu River and the stream of traffic on National Freeway 6. From the summit pavilion, the linked peaks of the Jiujiu Feng Nature Reserve are breathtaking. Nearby you can visit the Jiujiu Feng Eco-Art Park exhibition hall and the Yu-Hsiu Museum of Art.
forestry-165:
The Primeval Cypress Forest trail is in Taipingshan National Forest Recreation Area, a primeval cypress forest behind Taipingshan Villa. Reach it via the Red Leaf trail lined with purple-leaf maples; the walk starts behind Zhen'an Temple.

It's mostly boardwalk, among towering ancient trees in dense, misty shade — a cool forest bath on a hot summer day. Midway it connects to the Hemlock Forest nature trail.
forestry-170: The Jinshuiying National Trail runs from Shuidiliao in Fangliao Township, Pingtung, in the west to the Jialuoban village in Dawu Township, Taitung, in the east. Of all the old trails across the Central Range, it has the lowest crossing point, was the most heavily used and was used the longest. Many relics of the old trail remain, and its biodiversity and number of rare plants are among the highest in Taiwan — ferns and orchids especially. A trail rich in human history and remarkable natural scenery.
forestry-174: The Zhennan Temple trail, once called the Chishan trail, is behind Zhennan Temple on Shanhu Road in Liujia District, Tainan. About 990 m long, it is wide and gentle with little up and down — ideal for middle-aged and older walkers. Well signposted with beautiful, varied forest, it overlooks Wushantou Reservoir and the Liujia plain — a leisure trail for all ages. Midway there's a lovely stand of straight lemon-scented gums.
forestry-178: The Fushan trail is above the Fushan village in Alishan Township, Chiayi, entered from km 69 of Highway 18, at about 1,270–1,360 m. There's a pavilion at the entrance and a rest platform at 430 m. To the right of the platform, a stairway leads down to Fushan village; or continue straight, then turn right to join that stairway and loop back to the platform and on to the entrance — about 1,850 m in all, an easy trail whose two halves look quite different. Several trees along the way show burn scars: in February 2009 a fire broke out nearby, and this strip was cleared as a firebreak to protect Fushan village. Afterward trees were planted on both sides and it was made into an eco-trail.
forestry-179:
This trail was originally an old Tsou migration and contact route. After Typhoon Morakot badly damaged the Limei trail in 2009, villagers realized the old path could serve for emergency rescue and proposed its restoration to the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency. About 1.6 km long, it was named the Limei Evacuation Trail for that emergency use.

The upper part is mostly natural primeval forest, rich and intact; lower down, at lower altitude, signs of cultivation appear. Along the way are three wooden hunting huts in Indigenous style to rest in, several unusual triangular suspension bridges, and a viewing deck with an excellent view over Danayigu.
forestry-180: The Longlin Mountain trail in Tainan, once called the Tongtou Mountain trail, is on the Neiwushan range at Tainan's eastern edge, on the border of Nanhua District, Tainan, and Neimen District, Kaohsiung, and is part of the Wushan trail. The 2.3 km loop winds along the ridge, where giant boulders spread out one after another like dragon scales — hence the name (Longlin means "dragon scales"). The rocks form narrow, scaly ridges like a coiled dragon clinging to the mountain's back, making the hike thrilling and challenging — the trail's defining feature.
forestry-198: The Fenqihu Taiwan Incense Cedar Mother Forest trail in Zhuqi Township, Chiayi, is at about 1,400 m and consists mainly of century-old Taiwan incense cedars — lush, quiet and serene. To improve the visitor experience, in November 2016 the Chiayi branch added about 100 m of boardwalk and three viewing decks linking to the original trail, built elevated so as not to disturb the ecology, letting visitors better enjoy the forest's peaceful stillness.
forestry-200: The Shuishan trail, a newly opened hidden gem in Alishan National Forest Recreation Area, combines the heritage of the old Alishan Forest Railway with a visit to the giant Shuishan red cypress. Walking it feels like entering a forest time tunnel full of railway history — come and enjoy a journey that refreshes body and mind.
forestry-201:
The Antong Crossing Trail played an important military role in the last years of Qing rule. From then on it was the main route between Pushige and Chengguang'ao, busy with merchants, settlers and missionaries. In the Japanese era it was improved and renamed the Hongcuo crossing; the east section is about 3.8 km long.
The east section is in the middle of the Coastal Range. Enter via the Zhuhu irrigation farm road from Nanzhuhu in Zhuhu Village, Changbin Township, Taitung (km 92.5 of Highway 11); it's about a 10-minute drive to the trailhead, and about 6.1 km on foot from there to the end of the west section.
forestry-207:
The Jinshuiying historic trail runs about 47 km from Fangliao, Pingtung, in the west to Dawu, Taitung, in the east. It began as a Qing-era road for governing Indigenous areas; most of the west section was later replaced by the new Dahanlin forest road. The front section starts near the Xinkai nursery and ends at km 5.2 of the Dahanlin forest road, joining today's road.

It's easy all the way, passing dry-stone retaining walls and simple wooden bridges under dense green shade, with pavilions for rest — a favorite exercise spot for Xinkai villagers. Many Qing and Japanese-era relics remain near the trail.
forestry-208:
Amei Mountain is in the center of Green Island, Taitung, 276 m high — the island's second-highest peak, just 4 m lower than Huoshao Mountain — and the source of several streams that radiate out to the sea.

The gently rising steps and dirt path are easy, with insects, birds and butterflies all around and distance markers along the way. There's no summit marker, but the viewing deck has a 360-degree view of Huoshao, Niuzi and other peaks; on clear days you can even see the southern Central Range on Taiwan's main island, and look down over all of Green Island and its coastline — superb.
forestry-209: The Sea-View trail is beside the Dahu village on Green Island's east coast, briefly sharing the east trailhead of the Guoshan trail. Only 220 m long, it's a steep boardwalk — a little tiring, but you gain height fast and the views are excellent. It ends at a pavilion on the saddle, from which you can follow the ridge to Big Black Rock and Sail Rock, look down on the quiet harbor and Dahu village as they once were, and see the Sleeping Beauty and Pug rocks from another angle. Native plants and ferns line the way — lush and full of life.
forestry-212:
The Sakul trail is the most approachable trail on the outskirts of Hualien City. Built with eco-friendly methods using gravel and natural dirt paths, it's gentle and easy and shaded all the way — listen to the insects and birds and breathe in the forest; very pleasant.
It's a loop, so whichever way you start you'll easily reach the viewing deck at the midpoint, close to the 18 m Sakul Falls. The water below is crystal clear, and the energizing negative ions wash away the noise of the city.
forestry-214: When the Chianan Canal was built in the Japanese era, the engineer Hatta Yoichi — the "father of the Chianan Canal" — designed and supervised a water-diversion tunnel about 3.2 km long to keep Wushantou Reservoir from running dry, with an east and a west portal. Hikers once crossed Wushan Ridge from the west portal to Zengwen Reservoir, known as the "east–west portal hike." This route climbs from city road 175 up a steep farm road through longan orchards and then onto a mountain path, passing Zengwen Reservoir benchmark No. 50, power pylons and an orchid-tree forest with lovely scenery beneath it, then a large landslide face, finally leaving the trail at the east portal work station.

Yinghan (Tough Guy) Ridge, 616 m, is the highest peak of Guanyin Mountain; it got its name because the military police school once trained "tough-guy spirit" here. The grade is 14.87%, fairly steep (class 2), and the 1,563 m one-way route is mostly stone steps; at a slow pace it takes at least 60 minutes to reach the top, so it's rated a "training-level" trail, best for regular hikers or those in good shape. The forest is dense along the whole trail with rich plant life and shade everywhere, so it's not too hot even in summer — take breaks to enjoy the scenery.
